text: Panter and Eisty position technical lag as latent technical debt while conceding the constructs differ in origin: 'while TD arises from deliberate shortcuts, TL emerges passively through inaction'.
caveat: arXiv preprint of the TechDebt 2026 paper; section/page numbers must be re-verified against the ACM version before quoting in a submission

text: Their bridge from lag to debt is a compounding-interest argument: 'Just as unresolved TD accrues "interest" in the form of additional maintenance effort, TL compounds the cost of eventual updates. Delayed upgrades often require larger migrations, adjustments to dependent modules, and extensive retesting.'
caveat: arXiv preprint; this is the claim B-RQ2 tests empirically

text: The review's evidence base is 18 studies: 43 unique papers identified, 15 meeting the inclusion criteria, 3 added by snowballing, over 2015-2025, from ACM DL, IEEE Xplore, Scopus and Springer.
caveat: self-reported by the authors; the replication dataset is cited as ref [15] and has not been checked

text: The authors themselves flag that 'findings that equate newer with safer may overstate risk', and that most reviewed studies cover npm and Debian, so conclusions 'might not fully apply to less-studied ecosystems or niche technological environments'.
caveat: arXiv preprint; a game engine is exactly such a niche environment

text: Jeronimo Junior and Travassos report an 'interpretation overload regarding its definition, inducing to classify any issue occurring during the software development as TD.'
caveat: peer-reviewed tertiary study over 19 secondary studies; the statement is their synthesis, not a primary measurement

text: Their tertiary study carries an explicit Non-TD category: external software quality, software defects, lacking supporting processes, not implemented features and unfinished tasks are named as things called TD that are not TD.
caveat: they flag the Non-TD evidence as low density and groundedness, resting mainly on one secondary study (SSTD5)

text: Their separating criterion is temporal and internal: TD 'closely relates to internal software quality, primarily maintainability and evolvability', while defects and low external quality 'may be perceived by end-users and restrict software products essential operation' and are therefore not TD; TD 'will only be perceived in the future due to the required costs and efforts to maintain or evolve a software product.'
caveat: the criterion is attributed to Kruchten et al. and adopted by the authors

text: The study adopts the Dagstuhl Seminar 16162 definition as 'the most accepted among researchers' and uses it as the yardstick for deciding what counts as a TD item.
caveat: their characterisation of consensus, not an independent measurement of it

text: Javan Jafari et al. study 112,452 npm packages and classify the update strategy their dependents converge on: 54.2 percent balanced, 29.3 percent permissive, 6.7 percent restrictive, 9.8 percent unspecialised.
caveat: npm only; strategy is inferred from dependents' version constraints, not from developer statements

text: The paper frames restrictive constraints as a deliberate, community-converged choice explained by package characteristics - dependent count, age and release status are the highest influencing features - rather than as a defect or a debt.
caveat: our reading of their framing; they make no claim about technical debt either way

text: Yoshioka et al. find that of 404 projects released after the Log4j 1.x end-of-life announcement, 66.19 percent were new adopters of the deprecated version and only 44 (10.89 percent) transitioned to Log4j-Core 2.x.
caveat: MSR 2025 Mining Challenge short paper; counts come from the challenge dataset via the Goblin framework and are descriptive

text: Their own discussion concedes the cause is unmeasured, attributing continued use to 'a lack of awareness regarding the security risks' or 'a perception that migration is prohibitively costly or complex', and names a qualitative study of the reasons as future work.
caveat: interpretation offered without demand-side evidence; the paper measures adoption, not motivation

text: Lu frames technical lag as a condition to be resolved: 'the technical lags have not been systematically resolved by existing tools to keep dependencies up-to-date', and evaluates LagEase by how much lag it removes.
locator: S I and S IV, pp.241-242
caveat: two-page ICSE 2025 Companion paper, single author, 182 modules, no statistical evaluation

text: The same paper concedes the demand side in its first paragraph: libraries 'cannot always be guaranteed to be the latest versions due to several concerns, such as stability'.
caveat: stated as motivation for compatibility-aware upgrading, not as an argument that lag can be legitimate

text: Zozas et al. operationalise TD principal as remediation effort computed from static rule violations - the SQALE index of SonarQube, in minutes, aggregated to project level - over 19,636 releases of 105 JavaScript applications.
caveat: one of several competing quantifications; the authors themselves note no TD tool is recognised as state of the art

text: The paper that coined technical lag states outright that being outdated is not itself a defect: 'The fact that deployed components are outdated is not a problem in itself, but there is a price to pay for not being "as much updated as reasonable". [...] Therefore, a balance has to be maintained between "being up-to-date" and "keeping the good old working versions".'
caveat: the abstract of the coining paper; the same authors later develop lag as a risk indicator, so the position is not uniform across their corpus

text: Gonzalez-Barahona et al. frame technical lag as decision support, not diagnosis: the model measures 'how outdated a system is, with the aim of assisting in the decisions about upgrading in production'.
caveat: same source and caveat

text: Their formal definition makes lag a non-negative real-valued function of a deployment against a chosen reference distribution, parameterised by that reference and by the per-component lag function - TechLag(D,S) = LagAgg(Lag(d_i,s_i)) - with no cost, intent or obligation term anywhere in it.

In our forward-citation sweep of the two constitutive technical-lag papers (Gonzalez-Barahona et al. 2017 and Zerouali et al. 2019), restricted to 2022 onward, 45 works were retrieved and 13 of them (29 percent) carry security vocabulary in the title.
caveat: OpenAlex forward citations only, capped at 50 rows per seed sorted by citation count; title-only keyword match, so it undercounts security work with a neutral title

text: The formal technical-lag framework is parameterised by the deployer's own preference. Definition 1 gives the tuple (C, L, ideal, delta, agg) where 'ideal : C -> C is a function returning the "most preferred" component release (according to the user desiring to deploy a component) over a given one', and the text states 'ideal could be interpreted in different ways: most recent, most compatible, most stable, most secure, etc.'
locator: S4 and S4.1, Definition 1, pp.5-6 of 20
caveat: the framework is generic by design; the authors present the parameterisation as flexibility, not as a caveat about interpreting lag

text: Their own npm instantiation fixes that parameter to latest-always: 'We consider the ideal deployment as having the latest available release for all deployed package releases', and Definition 5 sets idealnpm(p) to the highest available version, which 'mimicks the choice of the npm package manager'.
locator: S1 p.2 and S4.2 Definition 5, p.7 of 20
caveat: this is the validation case study, not a claim that latest is universally ideal

text: They explicitly anticipate a major-version-bounded alternative: 'An alternative variant of idealnpm is to select the highest backward compatible version for a given package release, restricting the selection of higher releases to those corresponding to the same major release number only.'
locator: S4.2, Definition 5 footnote text, p.7 of 20
caveat: offered as a variant and not used in their study; under this variant a project on the newest release of an older major line has zero lag

text: Gonzalez-Barahona's 2020 revisit keeps freshness conditional: the conclusions open 'Being as much up to date as possible (with respect to the most recently available snapshot of source code) is an important goal for some kinds of applications', and the decision is framed as 'part of the tradeoff between been as much up to date as possible, and using tested, well inspected components'.
caveat: single-author exploratory workshop paper; the qualifier 'for some kinds of applications' is the load-bearing phrase and should be quoted with its sentence

text: The same paper names the condition under which currency is fundamental: 'There is a very common case when using up to date components is fundamental, and this is when developers of the application work in close relationship with upstream developers to implement the features they need, and fix the bugs they find.'
caveat: stated as a motivating case, not as a general criterion; it is nonetheless a demand condition in the coining author's own words

text: Cox et al. define freshness relative to what is wanted, not to what is newest: 'the term "freshness" is used to denote the difference between the used version of a dependency and desired version of a dependency', and they state that 'while there exist ways to estimate the costs of upgrading dependencies, there is currently no way to quantify the long-term benefits of upgrading'.
caveat: the benefit-quantification gap is a 2015 statement; check whether later work closes it before repeating it

text: Stringer et al. frame lag as a defect to be eliminated: keeping dependencies up to date is 'necessary to maintain software quality', and their conclusion is that 'Technical lag is prevalent but preventable across package managers', recommending tooling 'to minimise technical lag'.
caveat: 14 package managers via the libraries.io dataset; the normative claim is asserted, not tested

text: Decan et al. state the currency norm directly: 'In order to take full advantage of the benefits of this type of reuse, developers should keep their dependencies up to date by relying on the latest releases. In practice, however, this is not always possible, and packages lag behind'.
caveat: the 'not always possible' framing treats deviation as an inability rather than a decision; no demand-side data is collected

text: Zerouali et al. show lag tracking deliberate distribution policy: they measure five dimensions of lag over 140,498 Debian-based Docker images across OldStable, Stable and Testing, and find 'The amount of lag incurred depends on the type of Debian distribution and the considered lag dimension.'
caveat: the five dimensions are package, time, version, vulnerability and bug lag; the policy reading is ours - they present the comparison as a measurement result

text: MALTA (Panter and Eisty, arXiv 2603.10265, submitted to IEEE TSE) corrects technical lag on the SUPPLY side: it distinguishes 'resolvable technical lag, caused by delayed updates during active maintenance, and terminal technical lag, caused by upstream abandonment in which no update path exists', and reports that '62.2% of packages classified as Low Risk by Version Lag alone are reclassified as High Risk when MALTA signals are incorporated'.
caveat: arXiv preprint, not peer-reviewed at time of reading; a novelty check counts preprints regardless

text: The same paper comes closest to naming the parameter, without treating it as the deployer's: the six lag categories each measure 'against a different "gold standard" and provides a different perspective on the system TL'.
caveat: they read the multiplicity as complementary perspectives on risk, not as a preference that a debt inference would inherit

text: MALTA also puts feature-completeness in play, but on the upstream side only: 'Not all software that appears inactive is truly abandoned; some may be stable or "feature complete" and require minimal updates.' Their Sedentary category lumps abandoned, feature-complete and update-delayed packages together.
caveat: the observation is about the depended-on package, never about the depending project's own demand

text: Across the 126 works OpenAlex indexes containing 'technical lag', 'dependency freshness' or 'version lag' in title or abstract, no title states that lag's reference version is the deployer's preference or that debt inferences inherit a fixed reference. The closest is MALTA, which corrects the reference for upstream abandonment.
locator: full result set, sorted by publication year
caveat: title-level screening of a single index; abstracts were not read individually, and OpenAlex misses venues DBLP and ACM DL cover. This is not yet a novelty claim - see the pending ACM DL and Google Scholar checks

text: The ACM SIGSOFT Empirical Standard for Repository Mining lists as an antipattern 'unvalidated, uni-dimensional operationalizations of multidimensional constructs (e.g. using github stars as a proxy for popularity)', and requires as an essential attribute that a study 'uses previously validated measures, quantitatively assesses construct validity, or both'.
locator: RepositoryMining.md, Antipatterns and Essential Attributes / method
caveat: the standards are community guidance maintained on GitHub, not a binding venue policy; check whether the target venue adopts them

text: The General Standard makes 'names the methodology or methodologies used' an ESSENTIAL attribute, alongside 'methodology is appropriate (not necessarily optimal) for stated purpose'.
caveat: same caveat

text: Its reporting antipatterns include 'Unnecessarily dividing the presentation of a single study into many papers (salami-slicing)' and 'Reporting - together in one paper - several immature or disjointed studies instead of one fully-developed study'.
caveat: same caveat; both are risks the A/B/C split must answer explicitly

text: VEM has run for seven editions indexed in SBC OpenLib, 2019 to 2025, reaching its XIII edition in 2025, with between 5 and 14 papers per edition (2025: 10; 2024: 14; 2023: 5; 2022: 11; 2021: 11; 2020: 10; 2019: 12).

text: Lam, Dietrich and Pearce state the lag-to-debt bridge in 2020, six years before Panter and Eisty: 'The use of outdated dependencies is often described as technical lag - the time period, or "version distance", between the release of the version of a component it depends on, and that of the latest version. Technical lag can be considered to be a form of technical debt that accrues with the passage of time, as the world changes around the client.'
caveat: read from the arXiv version; verify locators against the ACM version. They also call lag 'an indicator of the resistance of developers to upgrade'

text: The same paper states the demand-side qualification explicitly, as a reason not to upgrade: 'the upgrade might not provide any immediate benefit to the client (paying technical debt diverts engineering effort from other tasks that may be more immediately needed - in other words, technical debt doesn't matter if one is about to declare bankruptcy)'.
caveat: stated as an aside in a position paper; no measurement, no operationalisation, and they do not revisit the lag metric in light of it

text: The demand-side observation that lag may cost nothing when the project has no need for the upgrade is NOT novel - Lam et al. published it in 2020. What remains unstated in everything read so far is the measurement argument: that technical lag's reference version is a free parameter defined as the deployer's preference, and that debt inferences drawn from lag inherit a reference fixed to latest-always.
caveat: based on ACM DL page-1 exports, the 126-work OpenAlex lag universe screened at title level, and 15 papers read in full; Scopus and Google Scholar are still unchecked

text: Scopus cited-reference searches on the two constitutive technical-lag papers returned 37 and 32 records for 2022 onward; the majority were already in our corpus and none states that lag's reference version is the deployer's preference or that debt inferences inherit a fixed reference.
locator: scopus_S3_1.csv and scopus_s3_2.csv, screened at title and abstract level
caveat: Scopus indexes title, abstract, keywords and references - not article full text; a paper making the argument in its body only would not appear

text: A Scopus title-abstract-keyword search for technical debt combined with boundary-work vocabulary (misconception, conceptual clarity, construct validity, overuse, misuse, conflation, not technical debt, rethinking) returned 13 records.
caveat: small result sets can reflect vocabulary mismatch rather than absence; ACM DL full-text search remains the better test, and it has only been run at page-1 depth

text: The Scopus S5/S6 export is a duplicate of the S4 result set: all 10 records are technical-debt boundary papers, with no dependency-freshness and no game-engine records. Neither the rational-staying query nor the game-engine query has been run.
locator: compared record by record against scopus_S4.csv
caveat: diagnosis from content, not from a Scopus error message; the user should re-run S5 and S6 separately

text: Pashchenko et al. already critique the technical-lag operationalisation in TSE: 'the proposed way to calculate the semantic technical lag is might be misleading as it by far overestimates the actual semantic difference between library versions. Therefore, claims that an increasing technical lag leads to more vulnerabilities needs to be reviewed with a correct definition of semantic technical lag.'
caveat: the critique targets the version-distance calculation, not the choice of reference version; the quoted sentence contains a typo in the original

text: The same paper names our research question as an open issue: 'An interesting issue that the paper [22] does not touch is automatically establishing when a particular project is lagging behind too far to warrant an action from the developers.'
caveat: stated as a gap in related work, not pursued by the authors; still open as of our 2026-08-26 sweeps

text: Vuln4Real structures its construct critique as a five-item taxonomy of how current approaches distort the picture: inflation of unexploitable vulnerabilities, underestimation of transitive vulnerabilities, imprecise vulnerability mapping, misrepresentation as somebody else's problem, and misreporting that nobody is in charge.
caveat: S1 Introduction, p.1592

text: Pashchenko et al. interviewed 25 developers in nine countries and report Observation 10, that 'developers avoid updating dependencies as they lack resources to cope with the breaking changes (possibly hidden in transitive dependencies) introduced by new dependency versions', and Observation 11, that 'company policy significantly affects developers decisions about updating software dependencies by splitting the field in two: adopt every new version or ignore all updates'.
caveat: semi-structured interviews with enterprise and SME developers; self-reported reasoning, not observed behaviour

text: The same study records exposure-conditional reasoning in developers' own words: some interviewees do not worry about dependency vulnerabilities because 'their projects are not security critical, i.e., used only for internal purposes, hence even if a vulnerability appears in their dependencies, they will not be exploited', and one developer summarises the prevailing attitude as 'If everything works, do not touch it'.
caveat: quotations are from interview transcripts already anonymised by the authors

text: Miller et al. find that among npm projects with development activity after a dependency was abandoned, only 18 percent ever removed the abandoned dependency (419 of 2,288); the vast majority did not.
caveat: excludes dependents that update automatically through floating version declarations, which the authors estimate would add about 33 percent immediate reactions

text: Miller et al. model time-to-removal with Kaplan-Meier survival analysis and right-censoring, on the grounds that 'survival analysis is designed to account for right-censoring' and for dependents that have had different amounts of time to react.
caveat: cited here as the method precedent for Paper A's survival curves

text: Cogo et al. report that 27 percent of all npm client packages directly adopt at least one deprecated release, that adoption of deprecated releases is highly skewed with the top 40 accounting for more than half of all adoption, and they derive five reasons for deprecation: withdrawal, supersession, defect, test and incompatibility.
caveat: npm only; deprecation is an explicit upstream act, unlike engine major releases

text: Across 13 papers read in full for this project, the number of numbered research questions ranges from none (a 2-page tool paper) to nine (a tertiary study). Short venues carry three: the 4-page MSR challenge paper and the 6-page TechDebt review both state RQ1-RQ3. Full conference and journal papers carry three to five. No paper in the set states a single research question.
locator: regex count of distinct RQ<n> labels in the stored full texts
caveat: counts labelled RQs only; a paper can pose questions in prose without numbering them, and Lu 2025 does exactly that

text: Of the 157 repositories in the GEM v0.1 history tier that were declaring Godot 3 at 4.0-stable and had not migrated by 2026-08-26, 71 carry at least one rule-detected demand signal and 86 carry none (45.2%, Wilson 95% CI [37.6, 53.0]). One of the 71 also carries the corpus's only counter-demand signal, so 70 have demand with no recorded objection.

text: Dormancy of the never-migrated cohort: median 1,506 days since last commit; only 16 of 157 (10.2%, CI [6.4, 15.9]) committed anything in the 365 days before observation. Of those 16 active repositories 12 (75.0%) carry a demand signal, against 59 of the 141 dormant ones (41.8%).
locator: derived over lag_observations.jsonl dormant_days joined to blocked_demand.jsonl, 2026-09-01

text: RQ2, no detectable association between time waited and migration churn: over 48 boundary observations in 41 migrating repositories, Spearman rho(duration_days, total boundary churn) = +0.084 (p=0.57), rho with .gd/.cs churn = +0.203 (p=0.17), rho with .tscn/.tres churn = +0.218 (p=0.14). Partial rank correlations controlling for pre_files are -0.070, +0.152 and +0.173. By contrast rho(pre_files, total churn) = +0.861 (p<0.001) and rho(pre_files, duration_days) = +0.139 (p=0.35).

text: GEM v0.1 instrument agreement: of 200 repositories in the validation study, 101 carry no secondary version signal and 65 carry only prose (README) hints; among the 34 with a machine-readable secondary signal the declared version agrees in 26 cases, a 76.5% agreement rate. 33 of the 34 machine-readable signals are CI pins; 1 export preset and 1 container tag.

PlayMyData (MSR 2024, DOI 10.1145/3643991.3644869) is 99,864 multi-platform commercial games mined from IGDB with descriptions, genres, ratings, 43,812 gameplay video URLs, 443,630 screenshots and HLTB completion times; it contains no source repositories, no commits and no engine version information.

After 4.0-stable (2023-03-01) and up to 2026-08-26, upstream shipped six stable releases on the Godot 3.x line: 3.5.2 (2023-03-07), 3.5.3 (2023-09-25), the first-of-minor feature release 3.6 (2024-09-09), and the patches 3.6.1 (2025-06-25), 3.6.2 (2025-10-23) and 3.6.3 (2026-08-22). 3.6 shipped 25 days after 4.3 (2024-08-15) and 3.6.3 shipped four days before the observation date. Over the same window the 4.x line received 25 stable releases, 8 of them first-of-minor.
locator: derived over releases.jsonl filtered on channel=stable and released_on > 2023-03-01, 2026-09-01
caveat: five of the six 3.x releases are patches; 3.6 is plausibly the terminal feature release of the line, so these establish that the line was maintained, not that it was still being developed

text: Godot 4.x first-of-minor stable release cadence: 8 releases (4.0 to 4.7) over 1,205 days, a median of 147 days apart (gaps 127, 147, 259, 200, 196, 133, 143). Lag measured against the newest available release therefore advances roughly twice a year independently of any project's behaviour.
locator: derived over releases.jsonl, line=4.x, is_first_of_minor, channel=stable, 2026-09-01
caveat: the mechanism behind the adopt-then-drift asymmetry: 239 of 917 Godot 4 projects sit at the maximum distance of 7 while 89 of 93 migrations landed on the newest release available that day

text: The Godot documentation describes the 4.0 transition as a rewrite: "Since Godot 4 is a complete rewrite in many aspects, some features have unfortunately been lost in the process."
locator: Upgrading from Godot 3 to Godot 4 > Caveats of upgrading

text: The Godot documentation states that the conversion tool is partial and leaves manual work: "the project upgrade tool cannot cater to all situations. Therefore, a large part of the upgrade process remains manual." After conversion "Scripts will likely contain various errors as well (possibly hundreds in large projects)" and "not all API renames can be performed automatically."
locator: Upgrading from Godot 3 to Godot 4 > Fixing the project after running the project upgrade tool

text: The Godot documentation frames the upgrade as conditional on wanting the new features: "If you don't need any features present in Godot 4.x, you may want to stay on Godot 3.x for the following reasons", listing higher baseline hardware requirements, larger exported binary size, and no GLES2 support.
locator: Upgrading from Godot 3 to Godot 4 > Disadvantages of upgrading

text: The Godot documentation bounds support of the old line: "Godot 3.x will continue to be supported for some time after 4.0 is released, but it will eventually stop receiving support."
locator: Upgrading from Godot 3 to Godot 4 > Advantages of upgrading

text: The conversion tool is exposed as two command-line flags on the Godot 4 editor binary, --validate-conversion-3to4 (dry run) and --convert-3to4, with default size limits of 4 MB and 100,000 lines: "If a file hits either of those limits, it will not be upgraded by the project converter."
locator: Upgrading from Godot 3 to Godot 4 > Using the command line

text: The Godot 2.x line last received a stable release on 2019-07-11 (2.1.6), seven years before the 2026-08-26 observation date. The 430 project files in the snapshot tier still declaring config_version=3 are therefore on a genuinely unmaintained line, unlike the 3.x cohort.
locator: releases.jsonl filtered on line=2.x and channel=stable, 2026-09-02
caveat: corrects an unsourced "last stable release was in 2017" written into an early results draft; the 2.x line received 12 stable releases, the last being 2.1.6

text: Unreal is instrumentable despite the GUID case: GitHub code search reports ~35,584 hits for EngineAssociation in .uproject files and 3,457 non-fork repositories under topic:unreal-engine; in a 60-file sample 56 carry a plain version string, 3 a local GUID and 1 is empty, with versions spanning 4.10 to 5.5 (most frequent 5.0 with 9 and 4.25 with 8).

text: Unity publishes a queryable release timeline: services.api.unity.com/unity/editor/release/v1/releases returns 1,566 releases with version, releaseDate and a stream field valued LTS, SUPPORTED or BETA.

Canella et al. mine 491 open-source video games from itch.io hosted on GitHub and report engine concentration: repository-based detection identifies Godot in 120 projects (24.4%) and Unity in 84 (17.1%), the two largest of 75 distinct engines and frameworks. Detection identified an engine in 260 of 491 projects (52.9%), so Godot and Unity together account for 78% of the projects where an engine was determined.
caveat: human-supplied PDF (ACM DL 403 to automation); artifact cannot be re-verified by re-fetching; itch.io + GitHub open-source games only

text: Canella et al. detect Godot by the presence of project.godot, the same file this paper's instrument reads, mapping each engine to characteristic file signatures (Unity: ProjectSettings/ProjectSettings.asset and *.unity; GameMaker: *.yyp; Construct: *.c3p).
caveat: human-supplied PDF (ACM DL 403 to automation); artifact cannot be re-verified by re-fetching; itch.io + GitHub open-source games only
